Front-facing lunge hold with arms overhead. Warrior II turns the hips and arms out to the sides, so the two are separate poses.
Hips and arms open to the sides, unlike Warrior I, which faces forward with arms overhead.
A single-leg balance with a hip hinge. Warrior I and II are lunges held on two legs.
Adds a side bend and overhead arc to the lunge. Warrior II keeps the torso upright with arms out to the sides.
Wide straight-leg stance with a sideways torso tilt. Extended Side Angle bends the front knee and sets the forearm on the thigh.
Adds a torso twist to the Triangle Pose. Triangle Pose faces forward with no twist.
Bends the front knee and sets the forearm on the thigh. Triangle Pose keeps the front leg straight.
A one-leg balance with the torso sideways and the free leg lifted. Warrior III is a forward-facing one-leg balance.
Kneeling lunge with the back knee on the floor. Warrior I is a standing version with the back heel lifted.
Feet together with arms overhead and a deep squat hold. Goddess Pose uses a wide stance and arms out to the sides.
A pure balance hold with the free foot placed on the standing leg. Eagle Pose wraps the legs and arms together.
Legs and arms wrap around each other for balance. Tree Pose keeps the arms free and only hooks the foot.
One-leg balance that holds the back foot and arches the spine. Tree Pose does not hold the foot or arch the back.
A low hold with elbows kept close to the body. A standard push-up repeats the movement and goes all the way down and up.
A hips-high inverted V with the heels pressing down. Upward-Facing Dog is the opposite, a back-arched position with the hips off the floor.
Lifts the chest and legs off the floor while lying face down. Cobra lifts only the chest and upper back.
Holds both ankles and lifts the chest and thighs at the same time. Locust keeps the arms free and lifts the legs straight.
A kneeling backbend with the hands reaching for the heels. Bow Pose is face-down with the ankles held.
A full backbend with the hands on the floor, not a bridge. Glute Bridge lifts only the hips and keeps the upper back on the floor.
Lies on the back and arches the upper chest. Wheel lifts the whole body off the floor.
Kneeling side bend with one leg straight out to the side. Side Lunge keeps both legs bent.
A seated twist with one leg crossed over. Revolved Triangle is standing and uses a wide stance.
Adds a backbend and a grip on the back foot to the Pigeon stretch.
A one-leg forward fold with the other knee bent. Seated Forward Fold uses both legs straight.
Stacked knees with arms stretched behind the back. Pigeon Stretch is a hip opener without arms behind the back.
Deep squat hold with the hands in prayer position. Chair Pose is a higher squat with arms overhead.
Balance on the head and forearms. Handstand is balanced on the hands only.
Lifts the hips and legs up with the body resting on the shoulders. Plow Pose lowers the legs behind the head.
Lowers the legs over the head from a shoulder stand. Shoulder Stand keeps the legs up in the air.
Balance on the forearms instead of the head. Headstand puts the head on the floor.
Standing forward fold with a wide stance. Standard standing forward fold uses a narrower stance.
Single-leg hamstring stretch with the free leg straight up in front. Half Moon keeps the lifted leg behind.
A restful inverted hold with the legs resting on a wall. Shoulder Stand lifts the hips and body off the floor.
Seated upright with both legs straight and feet flexed. Boat Pose lifts the legs off the floor.
Lifted head and shoulders with rapid arm pumping. Crunch curls the upper body without pumping the arms.
Rolls the hips over the head while the legs stay together. Roll-Up lifts the upper body from the floor with the legs straight.
Lying leg circle with the hips kept still. Hip Circles move the hips in a standing or prone position.
Rocks on the back in a tight ball shape. Roll Down moves the spine down one vertebra at a time with the legs straight.
Alternates one hugged knee and one extended leg with the head lifted. Dead Bug keeps the head down and moves the arms and legs opposite.
Hugs both knees in and sweeps the arms overhead and back. Single Leg Stretch moves only one leg at a time.
Rocks on the tailbone with the legs wide. Rolling Like a Ball rocks in a tight, closed ball shape.
Legs lifted and rolled together while lying down. Seated Corkscrew is done seated with the legs circling in a seated position.
Full prone arch with arm swings. Superman lifts the arms and legs off the floor together without a swinging motion.
Rocks on the sit bones with hands clapping by the feet. Seal Row is a rowing pull and is not a rocking motion.
Balanced V-shaped roll-up with arms reaching forward. Roll-Up keeps the legs flat or straight on the floor.
Hand-supported balance with the legs held in shape. Handstand is a full inverted balance held straight.
Lifts arms and legs together with fast alternating kicks. Bird Dog is slower and holds opposite arm and leg on all fours.
Kneeling side-lying kick with the upper body on a forearm. Side Kick is done lying on the side with a straight body.
Lying on the side in a straight line with the top leg kicking. Kneeling Side Kick is done on the knees with the upper body propped up.
Curls the upper body with the hands behind the head and the elbows pulling forward. Crunch curls without a sitting-up pull on the neck.
A multi-part sequence that adds a twist and leg change to a roll-up. Roll-Up is a single upward curl.
Seated hip rotation with the legs bent. Spine Twist keeps the hips still and rotates the upper body.
Single leg kick from the belly, with the other leg still on the floor. Double Leg Kick kicks both legs.
Kicks both legs together from the belly. Double-Leg Butt Kick is an upright cardio-style kick.
Bridge with one leg extended out in front. Glute Bridge keeps both feet on the floor.
Established weighted thumb-side wrist deviation differs in axis from the named palms-up wrist curl and reverse wrist curl; a generic wrist curl does not rule it out.
Established weighted little-finger-side wrist deviation has the opposite active direction from radial deviation; generic wrist curls do not rule out this directional variant.
Published research treats the razor curl and Nordic hamstring curl as distinct techniques, including different hip motion or positioning.
A kettlebell circles the head while the torso remains stable, an established distinct shoulder movement. The unspecified path of around-the-world-kettlebell is not evidence of equivalence.
The established weighted sequential spinal roll-down from elevation is an identifiable loaded and positioned variation of a generic bodyweight roll-down under the revised policy.
Forward alternating running bounds form a recognized straight-ahead drill, distinct by travel direction from the named diagonal and lateral bounds.
Repeated small two-foot ankle rebounds without a rope are an established distinct rope-free plyometric exercise from rope-assisted jumps.

The proposal uses forearm-and-toe support while moving forward. That is a substantive support distinction from the conventional hand-supported bear crawl; the generic spider-crawl name alone does not establish equivalence.
A named boxing footwork drill rapidly exchanges the feet close to the floor in a front-back stance. This defined technique may be kept as a specific variant of the general scissor-jump entries.
The wrist turns palm-up during the curl. A standard curl holds one grip throughout. Review: Catalyst Athletics has an individual exercise page and its instructions match the palm rotation described.

Uses a kettlebell held by the horn. An upright row is usually with a barbell or dumbbells. Review: Catalyst’s individual page supports the lift, but specifies holding the kettlebell with both hands at arm’s length, not by one horn. The broad source category should be replaced with the exercise page.

Done with one arm at a time. A ring row uses both arms. Review: The individual Catalyst page confirms the one-arm ring row. Preserve its key setup cues: body rigid and facing forward, leaning back from the rings, then pulling up.

Done one arm at a time. A Z-press uses a bar or two dumbbells. Review: Catalyst’s individual page supports the movement but also permits a dumbbell or kettlebell; its explicit position and bracing details are clearer than the current summary.

Both hands grip the bar end from underneath, like a two-handed press. A landmine press may be single-arm. Review: BarBend treats the Viking press as a named press using the lever/landmine implement; the proposal’s general press description is consistent, though it could be more specific about the implement handles.

The bar is held at the chest and angled across the body. A reverse lunge is usually done with dumbbells or a barbell. Review: BarBend’s individual instructions specify standing perpendicular to the landmine with the bar end in the elbow crease, then driving the rear knee up. Current description omits this identity-defining setup.
One arm with a leg drive. A landmine press uses no leg drive. Review: BarBend’s instructions match the one-arm landmine push press with a quarter-squat dip and drive.

Done on the floor with an arced bar path. A floor press uses a free bar or dumbbells. Review: The cited BarBend exercise is specifically a single-arm floor press: begin with both hands, then remove one hand and press unilaterally. Current text describes a different two-arm press.

The landmine counterbalances the load for a deep side squat. A cossack squat is done with bodyweight or a goblet hold. Review: BarBend specifies a goblet hold and lifting the toes of the straight leg while keeping its heel down; the proposal’s description misses both details.

The press arcs from side to side. A landmine press goes in one line. Review: BarBend describes alternating shoulder-to-shoulder by pressing through the center, rather than pressing up and over each side as stated here.

A jump with the bar held at the sides. A trap bar squat has no jump. Review: BarBend has a dedicated section and instructions for the trap-bar jump squat; it is distinct from a standard trap-bar squat.

Neutral-grip press with a trap bar. A barbell floor press uses a straight bar. Review: BarBend confirms a neutral-grip trap-bar floor press but specifies the bar is set on a rack, with flat handles down and D handles up. The current “lie inside the bar” setup is unsupported.

Back foot on a bench, with the trap bar held at the sides. A Bulgarian split squat uses dumbbells or a barbell. Review: The BarBend setup has only the front foot inside the trap bar and the back foot on a flat bench; the current description incorrectly says to stand inside the bar.

Staggered feet with a trap bar. A trap bar deadlift uses side-by-side feet. Review: BarBend confirms the B-stance variation but describes the rear foot as a kickstand and heel-toe turned out. The short description is broadly right but omits these defining cues.

Hip-hinge style with a trap bar and no floor reset. A trap bar deadlift is lifted from the floor. Review: BarBend says to pick up the bar with a deadlift first, then lower only to just below the knees or around the shins. Current description could imply starting each rep from the floor.

Pull from raised pins using a trap bar. A barbell rack pull uses a straight bar. Review: The BarBend setup specifies handles just below the knees in a power rack; “about knee height” is less precise and could put the bar too high.

One-leg hinge with a trap bar. A trap bar deadlift uses both feet. Review: BarBend’s sequence begins with both feet down to pick up the bar, then moves the non-working leg back and out of the bar’s path. Current description incorrectly begins by balancing on one leg.

Neutral-grip overhead press with a trap bar from a tall-kneeling stance. Review: BarBend’s individual instructions require the trap bar to be set on rack pins above shoulder height, rather than held at the shoulders from the floor.

Neutral-grip row with a trap bar. A barbell row uses a straight bar. Review: The BarBend page has a dedicated section. Its instructions row the bar until its back nearly touches the glutes; the current wording is a reasonable summary but should use the stated path.

Neutral grip from a multi-grip bar. A barbell bench press uses a straight bar with a pronated grip. Review: BarBend describes the Swiss-bar bench press with neutral-grip handles; the position and equipment identity are supported.
Neutral grip with a multi-grip bar. A barbell overhead press uses a straight bar. Review: BarBend’s individual exercise section confirms the overhead press uses the Swiss bar’s neutral grip.
Neutral grip with a multi-grip bar. A barbell row uses a straight bar. Review: BarBend’s instructions confirm the neutral-grip bent-over row; the proposal’s concise execution summary is sound.

Neutral grip, chest supported. A seal row uses a straight bar. Review: BarBend says the bar lies under a raised bench and the lifter rows face-down while keeping the body against the bench. The proposed floor-to-bench path does not match those instructions.

Done with a neutral-grip bar. A pullover is usually with a dumbbell. Review: BarBend’s dedicated section describes a Swiss-bar pullover from a bench with a slight, fixed elbow bend; proposal is consistent.
Done with a neutral-grip bar. A front raise uses dumbbells or a straight bar. Review: BarBend’s instructions raise the bar to chest level, not eye level.
Neutral grip. A skullcrusher uses an EZ bar or straight bar. Review: BarBend confirms the neutral-grip Swiss-bar skull crusher and the described elbow-extension action.
Hammer-style grip on a bar. A hammer curl uses dumbbells. Review: BarBend’s individual instructions match a Swiss-bar curl using the neutral hammer grip.

The bell changes hands at the top. A kettlebell swing keeps the same hand or both. Review: The Kettlebell Workouts library names the swing-changing-hands movement; the proposed alternating hand switch is identity-consistent.
The bell travels overhead. A Russian swing stops at chest height. Review: Motra’s individual page confirms a two-handed swing from between the legs to overhead.

The feet step sideways between swings. A normal swing stays in place. Review: The source supports a side-stepping swing, but its exercise uses lateral footwork as the bell swings; this description is broad and acceptable after noting the step occurs around the peak.

Uses two kettlebells on the floor and alternates rows. A kettlebell row is done with one bell. Review: PureGym’s exercise-specific instructions confirm two kettlebells in a hinged stance, one bell remaining grounded for support while the other is rowed, alternating sides. The proposal description matches.

The bell stays locked out above you as you roll. A Turkish get-up rises to standing. Review: The movement is real, but the broad exercise-list citation does not support the mechanics. NASM’s demonstration supports rolling to the side while keeping the loaded arm vertical; patch the description and citation.

Uses a kettlebell held by the horns. A pullover is usually with a dumbbell. Review: The movement is real, but the cited list does not substantiate mechanics. A strength-training source confirms the kettlebell is gripped by the horns from a supine position; current motion is a sound summary.

Moves in a side-to-side weaving pattern. A side lunge goes in one line. Review: The source supports a lateral dipping/side-to-side movement with the bell held at the chest. It does not support passing the bell under the knee; that mechanic appears invented.

The torso turns over the front leg. A plain lunge keeps the chest square. Review: The individual Kettlebell Workouts exercise page supports the lunge-with-rotation identity and the proposed torso rotation.

Combines a side lunge with a clean. Each is its own exercise. Review: A distinct exercise is verified, but its individual source describes a lateral step/lunge followed by cleaning the kettlebell as the lifter returns to start; the current “bell between feet, clean after standing” sequence differs.
The bell is held overhead, which adds a shoulder stability demand. Review: The source library and individual exercise page support holding a kettlebell overhead during a reverse lunge.
The bell is held overhead as you walk. A walking lunge holds the load at the sides or rack. Review: The source library supports this distinct walking-lunge position with the kettlebell overhead.

Pressed from a tall-kneeling stance, so the legs cannot help. Review: The kettlebell press manual gives the named tall-kneeling setup: kneel tall, clean the bell to rack, brace the glutes and press overhead. A distinct position from the standing press is supported.

Pressed from a half-kneeling stance. A standing press uses both legs. Review: The exercise-specific instructions confirm a one-knee-down stance, glute engagement, and overhead kettlebell press. Either arm/knee relationship is used, so the prior correction appropriately removes a fixed side prescription.

Combines a split-stance lunge with a press. A lunge and press may travel instead. Review: The exercise-specific demonstration confirms a fixed-foot split stance, a lower-and-rise lunge, and an overhead press during the rise. This is meaningfully distinct from the stepping lunge-and-press.

Pressed from the floor in a seated position. Seated presses on a bench use a back pad. Review: The individual exercise page confirms a supine start and simultaneous sit-up/overhead press with the kettlebell held in both hands. Catalog searches found a barbell Press Sit-Up and a seated kettlebell press, but no equivalent kettlebell sit-and-press; the equipment and movement distinction is real.

The weight stays locked out overhead through the sit-up. Review: The exercise-specific guide confirms the proposed pattern: start supine with legs straight and the bell over the chest, sit up with the arm locked, then lower while keeping it overhead. This is distinct from the sit-and-press, which presses while sitting up.

Squats to the floor and rolls back before standing. A kettlebell squat stays on the feet. Review: The exercise-specific demonstration confirms the described kettlebell deck squat: hold the bell at chest height, squat and roll onto the back, then use a forward swing to sit up and stand.

Cleaned while balancing on one leg. A kettlebell clean uses two feet. Review: Motra’s individual instructions confirm the one-leg clean and explicitly specify the opposite hand gripping the bell. The original proposal’s contralateral setup is supported; it is distinct from an ordinary one-arm clean.

You face the pad rather than leaning your back on it. A hack squat has your back on the pad. Review: Westside’s individual article supports the reverse hack squat, with the lifter facing the machine pad.
